newsitem.title: PERU: Mothers drop bid to mediate in Peru hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Mothers drop bid to mediate in Peru hostage crisis.

text.p: Ignored by the government and barred from meeting with hostages or jailed rebels, one of Latin America's best known human rights groups on Friday gave up trying to mediate in Peru's 74-day siege at the Japanese ambassador's home.

But the delegation from the Buenos Aires-based Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo, which has tried all week to play a role in talks between the government and Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages, said it would charge Peru with human rights abuses.

"(The Mothers) are going to present a formal complaint (to international bodies) against the Peruvian government for its prisons and political prisoners," Hebe de Bonafini, the group's leader, said. Repeated rebuffs by President Alberto Fujimori have forced the delegation to announce its return to Argentina on Sunday.

The government and the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels holed-up at the ambassador's residence have held a series of face-to-face talks over the last week to hammer out a peaceful solution to the crisis.

The rebels stormed the residence on Dec. 17 in a bid to force the government to free about 400 jailed comrades, whom they claim are living in inhuman conditions. They also demand an end to Peru's secret military court system that tries people accused of terrorism without allowing cross-examination of witnesses.
The next talks are scheduled for Monday, allowing the two sides to study suggestions put forward by the negotiations' guarantors for a bloodless end to the siege.
Following the last meeting on Thursday the guarantors were upbeat about progress in the talks, saying they "noted and appreciated the desire of the participants to achieve a solution."
Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent said the guarantors had also made concrete suggestions to the two sides. But, bound to secrecy on exactly what is discussed at the talks, he did not give details.
"During this meeting, substantial issues continued to be addressed and for its part the commision of guarantors has listened to the discussions and put forward certain suggestions," he said.
The other guarantors overseeing the talks to end the crisis are the Red Cross and the Vatican.
President Alberto Fujimori has repeatedly ruled out considering the release of MRTA prisoners.

Fujimori has said he will use force to end the siege only if harm is done to the remaining captives, who include his brother, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia, two government ministers and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
